title: Man shot dead by Manitoba First Nations police had breaks with reality: inquest report
subtitle: Benjiman Richard, 23, was shot 5 times by police after he fired at officers in 2019
article: A man who was shot by police on Long Plain First Nation in 2019 was coping poorly with traumatic losses and had breaks with reality before his death, a Manitoba provincial court judge says.

"Benjiman Richard's final moments do not reflect or change the gentle soul [family and friends] knew and will love forevermore," provincial court Judge Shauna Hewitt-Michta wrote in her inquest report.
Benjiman Richard, 23, was shot five times by Manitoba First Nations Police on April 2, 2019, after officers responded to a report that he was firing a gun inside and outside his home.

In the years before his death, Richard lost formative members of his family. His father died in 2015 of an illness that started when Richard was a teenager, and a cousin, who was a close friend, and an uncle died 10 days apart in 2018, Hewitt-Michta wrote in the report released publicly on Wednesday .
"He had difficulty coping with these deaths and did not attend the funerals. He began associating with negative influences and increasingly lost himself in the drug subculture," the report said.
"His family began noticing changes in his behaviour and his mental wellness, including episodes of seeming disassociation and confusion about where he was or how he got there."
Tammy Smith, Richard's cousin, told the judge that a week or two before his death, his mother, Louise Richard, called Smith for help because Benjiman was unresponsive as he wandered around the house.
When relatives tried to interact with Richard, he covered his ears and hummed.
A few days before his death, Smith came home and found Richard at her house, sitting in a corner and slapping himself in the face with both hands.

Smith took his hands and told him to stop, but Richard didn't answer when asked what was wrong. Eventually, he seemed to become more aware of reality and asked Smith how he got to her house, the report said.
He told Smith he had spent the previous evening drinking with her brother - his cousin who had died a year earlier.

Sgt. David Kelly Keith, who is currently serving with the Ste. Anne Police in Manitoba, testified at the inquest that the First Nations Police Service's use of force policy closely mirrors police policies across the country.
He believes police used justifiable force when they shot and killed Richard, who was firing at them and had discharged his gun a number of times inside the house he shared with his mother.
Richard's blood alcohol level was more than two times over the legal limit for driving and he had also consumed cannabis, the inquest report said.
Police said they tried to speak to Richard, to identify themselves as police and ask him to stop, but he walked out of the house, aimed his gun and fired at them before they finished their sentences.
"The officers reasonably articulated fear of imminent danger from grievous bodily harm or death, and that all other police officers in similar circumstances would share that fear," the report said.
"Their decision to shoot was reactive to Benjiman Richard's behaviour."

On the day of the shooting in 2019, the Long Plain First Nation detachment of the police service was dealing with a number of challenges, including ongoing staff shortages and communications technology issues.
There were five police officers serving the area, including the sergeant, the inquest report said. Single officer shifts were common.
An hour before the call came in, the responding officer was working alone. An hour after the call, there were two officers scheduled to be on duty.
It was only because the 911 call coincided with a shift change that three police officers were available to respond.
"Calls for service involving discharge of a firearm are serious. The situation was dangerous for police, for Benjiman and Louise Richard and for the community," the inquest report said.

"The three responding officers were limited in the scope of their response by their number. They therefore prioritized containing Mr. Richard. With more officers, objectives like cautioning or evacuating neighbouring residences and enhanced interaction with dispatch may have been more feasible."
Since the shooting, staffing at the detachment has increased to nine officers, which means there are always two officers on shift, both day and night.
There were also technology challenges for the three responding officers.
Cell reception was poor or non-existent in some areas of the First Nation. Dispatch information didn't always come through to officers in Long Plain, or calls would be cut off or drop.
MTS made updates to benefit emergency services two years later, including better satellites and more towers. Now all officers in Manitoba use the same radio equipment.
Although Judge Hewitt-Michta declined to make any recommendations in the inquest, she said rural and remote police forces have challenges in safely carrying out their work.
"It is important they have access to the resources, human and otherwise, to realistically and safely meet their obligations."
